title: 2 Chronicles 33:21–25
context: Amon, Manasseh’s son, follows his father’s idolatry but does not humble himself as Manasseh had, and after two years his servants assassinate him. The people of the land execute the conspirators and make Josiah king (compare 2 Kings 21:19–26).

verses.text: Amon was twenty-two years old when he began to reign; and he reigned two years in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Amon begins to reign at twenty-two and reigns two years. Arminian readers see a brief reign that will repeat his father’s early sins without his later humbling.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the regnal summary introducing Amon. The account parallels 2 Kings 21:19, though the Chronicler omits his mother’s name.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, as did Manasseh his father; and Amon sacrificed to all the engraved images which Manasseh his father had made, and served them.
verses.arminianNotes: Amon “did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, as did Manasseh his father” and sacrificed to Manasseh’s engraved images. Arminian readers see Amon choosing to follow his father’s idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the evil continued. The mention of images Manasseh had made shows that some remained to be used, despite Manasseh’s removal of idols from the temple.

verses.text: He didn’t humble himself before the LORD, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself; but this same Amon trespassed more and more.
verses.arminianNotes: “He didn’t humble himself before the LORD, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself; but this same Amon trespassed more and more.” Arminian readers see a son who refused the path of repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the contrast with Manasseh’s humbling. The Chronicler uses the language of humility as a measure of each king, and Amon fails that test.

verses.text: His servants conspired against him, and put him to death in his own house.
verses.arminianNotes: His servants conspire and kill him in his house. Arminian readers note the violence of the coup, recorded without stating the conspirators’ motives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the assassination reported soberly, as in 2 Kings 21:23. Readers in this tradition avoid speculating about motives the text does not give.

verses.text: But the people of the land killed all those who had conspired against King Amon; and the people of the land made Josiah his son king in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: The people of the land kill the conspirators and make Josiah king. Arminian readers see the community acting to preserve the Davidic succession.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s providence preserving David’s line. The verse introduces Josiah, whose reforms are described in the next chapter.
